previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Strip HTML tags using JavaScript

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
I've often found myself in need of stripping HTML tags from a string. This is a common task when working with web content, and it's often necessary to remove tags to get the raw text. All you really need is a carefully crafted **regular expression**, such as `/\<[^>]*\>/g`, to match and remove all HTML tags from a string. This expression matches the **opening bracket** of a tag, followed by **any number of characters** that are not the closing bracket, and finally the **closing bracket**. The `g` flag makes sure that all matches are removed, not just the first one. You can then easily combine this regular expression with `String.prototype.replace()` to remove all HTML tags from a string. As a bonus, this also works for XML tags, which might also come in handy from time to time. ```js const stripHTMLTags = str => str.replace(/<[^>]*>/g, ''); stripHTMLTags('

lorem ipsum

'); // 'lorem ipsum' ``` --- Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/strip-html-tags.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: A JavaScript helper removes substrings matching HTML tags with a regular expression. Why must its output not be treated as sanitized HTML?
back: Removing apparent tags is a text transformation, not a security guarantee. HTML parsing includes malformed markup, entities, attributes, and context-dependent rules that a simple tag regex does not model. If the goal is to display user input literally, put it into a text sink such as an element's textContent or ordinary React text children. If the product intentionally permits HTML, use a maintained sanitizer configured for that output context. **Check:** Render `` as text in a disposable test and verify it stays visible text, not an element. Do not insert a home-grown tag stripper's output with innerHTML. --- Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/strip-html-tags.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.back:

Collapsible content React components — Tabs

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: A React component looks like tabs but is only a row of buttons that hides panels with CSS. What interaction and accessibility contract is still missing before it can be called an accessible tab widget?
back:
A tab widget needs coordinated tablist, tab, and tabpanel roles; selected-state reporting; connections between each tab and its panel; and a defined keyboard focus model. Horizontal tabs normally use Left/Right arrows to move among tabs, with activation following a deliberate automatic or manual policy.

Use an established accessible tabs component when available. Styling an active button is not enough, and filtering children by a function's name is fragile under wrappers and production transforms. Use explicit item data with stable IDs.

**Check:** Navigate with Tab and arrow keys, activate each tab, and verify the selected state, focused control, and visible associated panel. Test a single tab and dynamically removed items too.

---

front: A carousel computes (index + 1) % items.length. What must it do when items is empty, and what behavior should a one-item carousel expose?
back:
Handle an empty collection before using modulo; modulo zero produces NaN. Render an empty state with no enabled navigation. For one item, show the item and disable or omit navigation that cannot change the result.

For larger collections, keep a valid selected identity when items are removed or reordered, use labeled native buttons, and provide a visible position such as '2 of 4'. Auto-rotation adds pause and focus requirements and is unnecessary for a basic carousel.

**Check:** Test zero, one, and several items, then remove the selected item. No render should access an undefined slide or report an impossible position.

---

front: A tooltip appears only on mouse hover. Keyboard users cannot discover it. What behavior and content restrictions should the tooltip have?
back:
Show supplementary tooltip text when its trigger receives keyboard focus as well as hover, connect it through aria-describedby, and allow Escape to dismiss it. The trigger still needs its own accessible name.

Keep interactive controls out of a tooltip; use a popover or dialog when the content needs focusable actions. Essential instructions should be persistently available rather than discoverable only through a tooltip.

**Check:** Reach the trigger using Tab, confirm the description is associated with it, dismiss with Escape, and verify that the control still has a meaningful name without the tooltip.

---

front: A button already has the accessible name 'Export backup'. Supplementary explanatory text has id='export-help'. Which attribute connects the button to that description without replacing its name?
back:
Use aria-describedby="export-help" on the button.

```jsx
<button type="button" aria-describedby="export-help">Export backup</button>
```

The referenced text supplements the visible name. aria-labelledby would instead supply the accessible name, which is a different requirement. ID references must point to the intended content and remain unique.

**Check:** Inspect the accessibility tree: the name should still be 'Export backup' and the description should contain the help text.

Keep the error available until the user resolves or dismisses it. Preserve the draft, state what failed, and provide a retry when appropriate. Use a live-region pattern such as role="alert" for an important new error without unexpectedly moving keyboard focus. ```jsx

previous.front:
What happens when you try to run TypeScript directly in most JavaScript environments?

**A.** It throws a compiler error.

**B.** It automatically compiles to JavaScript.

**C.** It cannot run.

**D.** It runs normally without any issues.
previous.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Answer

**C.** It cannot run.

## Lesson context

JavaScript is considered a dynamically-typed language. This means that variables can receive any values at run time - declaring a variable as a number does not prevent you from assigning it a string value later, and function parameters can be passed any value.

The challenge of a dynamically-typed language is that the lack of type safety can introduce errors if you are not careful. TypeScript extends the JavaScript language to include static typing, which helps catch those errors before you even deploy your code. But how does it work?

Consider this JavaScript function:

```js
const getRandomValue = (array) => {
  return array[Math.floor(Math.random() * array.length)];
}
```

Our `getRandomValue` function takes an array and returns a random value from that array. But because JavaScript does not validate types, there is nothing preventing you from calling the function with a number:

```js
console.log(getRandomValue(10));
```

The console output for the current example will return `undefined` because it was expecting an array instead of a number.

But with TypeScript you can define a type for the array parameter:

```js
const getRandomValue = (array: string[]) => {
  return array[Math.floor(Math.random() * array.length)];
}
```

This type definition tells TypeScript that the array argument must be an array of strings. Then when you call `getRandomValue` and pass it a number, you get a different type of error called a compiler error.

Most JavaScript runtime environments, such as a browser or Node.js, cannot run TypeScript natively. Instead, you first need to compile, or translate, TypeScript code into regular JavaScript. You can do that with the built-in compiler that comes with the TypeScript language. When you run the compiler, TypeScript will evaluate your code and throw an error for any issues where the types don't match - such as passing a number into a function that expects an array.

You'll learn more about how these types work in the next few lessons. But it's this extra safety that makes TypeScript an appealing language for many developers and organizations.

---
